name: Britain: Migration, Empires and the People
subtitle: Vikings to Windrush: a thousand years of arrivals, departures and empire.

teaching_brief.unit_overview: A thematic study covering c790 to the present — the longest sweep on the spec, around 1,200 years. Students trace how invasion, settlement, migration and empire have shaped Britain's people and identity. The four AQA-named parts run chronologically: Conquered and Conquerors (Vikings to the Hundred Years' War), Looking West (sugar, slavery, North America, Huguenots, Highland clearances, Ulster), Expansion and Empire (India, Africa, Irish/Jewish migration, internal migration), and Britain in the 20th Century (end of empire, Windrush, Commonwealth migration, Europe). Throughout, students weigh seven named factors: war, religion, government, economic resources, science and technology, ideas (imperialism, social Darwinism, civilisation), and the role of individuals. The unit assesses second-order concepts of significance, similarity and difference, change over time, and the interplay of factors.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students believe migration to Britain is essentially a post-1948 (Windrush) phenomenon — the longest unit on the spec is precisely a corrective to this. Black presence in Britain pre-dates Windrush by centuries; the unit begins in c790 with Viking arrivals.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: David Olusoga, Black and British: A Forgotten History (Pan Macmillan, 2016/2021); BBC documentary series of the same name; AQA spec rationale 3.3.2 AC

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students conflate the three terms and use them interchangeably. The spec demands precision: empire (the political system of rule), colonialism (the practice of settling and exploiting territory), imperialism (the ideology justifying expansion, including social Darwinism and 'civilising mission').
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA spec line 1333 explicitly names imperialism and social Darwinism as factors students must distinguish; AQA principal examiner reports flag this on 16-mark factor essays

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students treat 'British' as a fixed identity that migrants joined or threatened. The spec's framing — 'how the identity of the people of Britain has been shaped by their interaction with the wider world' — is that British identity is itself the product of repeated migration (Anglo-Saxons, Vikings, Normans, Huguenots, Irish, Jews, Caribbean, South Asian).
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA spec lines 1312-1317; David Olusoga's argument in Black and British (2016) that British history has always been multicultural

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.topic: Windrush as the 'start' of Black British history
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students treat 22 June 1948 as Year Zero for Black Britain. In fact people of African descent have been documented in Britain since the Roman period, with established communities from the 1500s. Olusoga: post-war migration was unprecedented in scale but did not mark the beginnings of Black British history.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: David Olusoga, Black and British (2016/2021 edition with new chapter on Windrush scandal); Royal Museums Greenwich and BBC documentary commentary

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students present the Atlantic slave trade as a natural extension of European exploration rather than a deliberate, contested, profit-driven system that abolitionists campaigned against for decades before the 1807 Slave Trade Act and 1833 Slavery Abolition Act.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: Historic England Timeline of the Transatlantic Slave Trade and Abolition; UK Parliament Heritage Collections on the Transatlantic Slave Trade

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.topic: Empire as economically beneficial to all
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students assume empire enriched Britain straightforwardly and improved colonised societies. The historiography is contested: Niall Ferguson's case for empire's modernising effects sits against Caroline Elkins, Shashi Tharoor and others on famine, dispossession, the Bengal famine, the Mau Mau detentions and the long economic drain on India.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: Niall Ferguson, Empire: How Britain Made the Modern World (2003); Caroline Elkins, Britain's Gulag (2005) and Legacy of Violence (2022); AQA examiner reports flag students writing one-sided defences or condemnations

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Essays often Anglocentrically describe what was 'done to' migrants without showing migrants' own agency — Claudia Jones founding the West Indian Gazette and the indoor Caribbean Carnival in 1959 (response to the 1958 Notting Hill attacks), Gandhi's Indian National Congress strategy, Nkrumah's Convention People's Party, Kenyatta's KANU.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA examiner reports on 16-mark factor essays; The National Archives 'Empire Windrush: The Notting Hill Carnival' resource on Claudia Jones

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 8-mark significance question rewards both significance at the time and significance over time. Students who only address the immediate impact of an event (e.g. Windrush 1948 docking at Tilbury) cap themselves; top-band answers also explain its long-term legacy (1981 Nationality Act, 2018 Windrush scandal, Notting Hill Carnival, multicultural Britain).
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section A 8-mark significance questions (8145/2A/C series)

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 16-mark factor essay names ONE factor (e.g. 'war', 'government', 'role of individuals') and asks students to weigh it against others. Top-band answers explicitly address the named factor across at least two of the four AQA parts and reach a substantiated overall judgement — not a list of factors with no comparison.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2 Paper 2 Section A; AQA examiner reports flagging factor-list responses as a recurring issue

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 4-mark 'similar or different' question requires TWO ways and concrete supporting detail from across the period, not generic claims. Comparing across vastly different periods (Vikings vs Windrush, Huguenots vs Ugandan Asians) is consistently the hardest comparison skill at GCSE.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA spec section 4.4.2; Cambridge Assessment Network research on history examinations highlighting comparative judgement as the hardest GCSE skill

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 8-mark 'explain a development' question rewards causal narrative with consequences, not pure description. A development is a process across time (e.g. how the East India Company's role developed from trading post to political ruler) — students who narrate without explaining the consequences of each stage cap below the top band.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section A 8-mark explain-a-development questions

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Students must use specialist historical vocabulary (Danelaw, sepoy, abolitionist, dominion, Commonwealth, imperialism) accurately to access SPaG marks and the top mark band on extended responses.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA spec section 4.4.3 SPaG performance descriptors

teaching_brief.exam_paper_context: This is a Paper 2 Section A thematic study, examined alongside the British depth study (Section B) in a 2-hour Paper 2 worth 84 marks total. The thematic component is worth 40 marks (plus 3 SPaG), assessed through four question types: 4-mark Two Ways Similar or Different, 8-mark Explain Significance, 8-mark Explain a Development, and 16-mark Factors Essay (the named-factor judgement). All four questions span the full c790-present period, so students cannot get away with revising only one part of the unit.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Alfred the Great
key_individuals_and_groups.role: King of Wessex (871-899) who fought back the Viking 'Great Heathen Army' and negotiated the Danelaw, anchoring early English identity

key_individuals_and_groups.name: King Cnut
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Danish king of England (1016-1035) ruling a North Sea Empire spanning England, Denmark and Norway, illustrating Viking integration

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Emma of Normandy
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Queen consort to both Æthelred and Cnut, central figure linking Anglo-Saxon, Norman and Scandinavian power networks

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Henry II
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Angevin king (1154-1189) who launched the 1171 invasion of Ireland, beginning long English involvement in Ireland

key_individuals_and_groups.name: King John
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Lost Normandy and most Angevin continental holdings (1204), narrowing the kingdom toward an island identity

key_individuals_and_groups.name: John Hawkins
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Elizabethan privateer; first English trader of enslaved Africans (three voyages, 1562-67) — origin point of British involvement in Atlantic slavery

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Sir Walter Raleigh
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Promoter of Roanoke colony (1585) — early English colonisation of North America

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Pilgrim Fathers
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Religious migrants on the Mayflower (1620) establishing Plymouth Colony; example of religion as a migration push factor

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Robert Clive
key_individuals_and_groups.role: East India Company commander; victory at Plassey (1757) made the Company the dominant power in Bengal

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Warren Hastings
key_individuals_and_groups.role: First Governor-General of Bengal (1772) who consolidated Company rule and expanded its army

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Mangal Pandey and the Sepoys
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Indian soldiers whose grievances (greased cartridges, religious fears, annexation of Oudh) sparked the 1857 Indian Rebellion / Great Uprising

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Cecil Rhodes
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Mining magnate and Cape Colony PM whose 'Cape to Cairo' ambition drove southern African expansion and helped trigger the Second Boer War

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Mahatma Gandhi
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Leader of Indian nationalist movement using non-violent civil disobedience; key driver of 1947 Indian independence

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Kwame Nkrumah
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Convention People's Party leader; first Prime Minister of Ghana (1957), the first Sub-Saharan African colony to win independence

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Jomo Kenyatta
key_individuals_and_groups.role: KANU leader; first Prime Minister and President of independent Kenya (1963); imprisoned during the Mau Mau emergency

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Idi Amin
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Ugandan president whose 1972 expulsion order sent 27,200 Ugandan Asians to Britain in 90 days

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Claudia Jones
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Trinidadian-born activist; founded West Indian Gazette and the indoor Caribbean Carnival (1959) in response to the 1958 Notting Hill attacks

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Sam King and the Windrush passengers
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Among the 492 Caribbean migrants on HMT Empire Windrush (June 1948), often treated as the symbolic start of Commonwealth migration

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Vikings (Danes and Norse)
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Eighth-to-eleventh century raiders, traders and settlers who created the Danelaw and integrated into Anglo-Saxon society

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Hanseatic merchants
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Medieval German trading league based at the London Steelyard until expelled by Elizabeth I in 1597 — example of mercantile migration

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Huguenots
key_individuals_and_groups.role: French Protestant refugees fleeing Louis XIV's Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685); brought silk-weaving, banking and craft skills

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Highland clearances tenants
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Scottish Gaels evicted from estates (c1750-1860) who migrated to Lowland cities, North America and Australia

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Ulster Scots planters
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Lowland Scots and English settlers in the seventeenth-century Ulster Plantation, with long political consequences

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Irish famine migrants
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Around one million who fled the Great Famine (1845-49) to Britain, settling Liverpool, Manchester, Glasgow, London

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Eastern European Jewish migrants
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Approximately 150,000 (1881-1914) fleeing pogroms; settled East End, Manchester, Leeds; precipitated the 1905 Aliens Act

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Ugandan Asians
key_individuals_and_groups.role: 27,200 admitted to Britain in 1972 after Amin's expulsion; built businesses across the East Midlands and London

key_individuals_and_groups.name: EU A8 migrants
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Polish, Lithuanian and other Central/Eastern European citizens who migrated after the UK chose not to apply transitional restrictions to the 2004 enlargement — central to the Brexit migration debate

gaps.gap: Medieval Jewish communities and the 1290 Edict of Expulsion are implied by the spec's c790-present framing and 'migration to and from Britain' theme but are not named in any Part 1-4 bullet. Lesson 5 ('Medieval Migrants: Hanseatic Merchants, Jews & Lombards') covers this as a bridging lesson because examiners reward students who can compare medieval migration to later waves on the 4-mark similar/different question. Confirmation needed from Tom that this lesson is in scope.

The spec lists imperial 'propaganda' but examiner reports rarely cite specific case studies. Suggested teaching exemplars (the Rhodes Colossus 1892 cartoon, Empire Day 1902, music-hall jingoism) are conventional but not named in spec bullets. Tom may wish to specify if alternative exemplars are preferred.

Sensitivity content: the slave trade (Lesson 6), the Indian Rebellion's reprisals (Lesson 9), the Boer War concentration camps (Lesson 10), the Mau Mau emergency (Lesson 12), and the Windrush scandal (Lesson 13) all require careful handling. Approach is to engage critically without sanitising, following AQA's own course-design rationale and the historiographical balance between Ferguson and Elkins/Olusoga. No content removed, but tone notes may be needed at content-generation phase.
AQA does not require a named historic environment site for thematic studies (only for Section B British depth studies). historic_environment_site_2026 is therefore null.
